value.overview: The Fiery-billed Aracari is a small, colorful toucan of the Pacific lowlands of southern Costa Rica and western Panama. It is named for its vivid orange-red bill, which has a yellowish tip and dark basal markings. This social forest bird usually travels in small groups through the canopy, feeding mainly on fruit. It also takes insects and other small animal prey, especially when raising young, and helps disperse seeds through its movements and feeding habits.
value.classification: The Fiery-billed Aracari belongs to the toucan family Ramphastidae and the genus Pteroglossus. It is generally treated as a distinct species and has no widely recognized subspecies.
value.identification: Adults have mostly black upperparts, a red face, yellow underparts, and a broad red band across the lower breast and belly. The large bill is especially distinctive: the maxilla is orange to fiery red, fading toward yellow or greenish yellow near the base, while the basal bill and mandible are dark. A pale line surrounds the bill base. Juveniles are duller, with darker, browner plumage and less sharply defined breast markings. It is smaller and more brightly billed than the Collared Aracari.
value.rangeHabitat: The Fiery-billed Aracari has a restricted range on the Pacific slope from central and southern Costa Rica into western Panama, including the Chiriquí region. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the central and southern Pacific lowlands, extending north locally to the Orotina and upper Atenas areas, and usually occurring from sea level to about 1,500 meters. It uses humid evergreen forest, secondary woodland, forest edges, clearings, gallery forest, and wooded areas that retain mature fruiting trees.
value.migrationStatus: Resident and generally non-migratory in Costa Rica. It may make short local movements in response to fruit availability, but it is not a regular long-distance migrant.
value.breeding: Breeding in Costa Rica generally occurs during the first part of the year, with records concentrated from January through April and some broader reports extending into August. The nest is usually a natural cavity or an old woodpecker hole, commonly several meters above the ground. Two eggs are laid. The pair incubates and begins parental care, while other group members may help feed nestlings and remove waste after hatching.
value.dietFeeding: Fruit forms the main part of the diet. In Costa Rica, documented foods include fruits of Spondias, palms such as Bactris and Iriartea, Piper, Palicourea, Citharexylum, Ficus, Cecropia, Schefflera, papaya, banana, and guava. The species also eats insects, spiders, and other invertebrates, along with occasional small vertebrate prey, eggs, or nestlings. Animal food becomes particularly important while adults are feeding young.
value.behavior: Fiery-billed Aracaris are active, arboreal, and social, commonly moving through the upper forest and adjacent clearings in loose groups of up to about ten birds. They call frequently while traveling and often perch conspicuously on exposed branches. Groups may cooperate around nest cavities, with additional adults helping deliver food and clean the nest. Their fruit-eating behavior makes them useful seed dispersers in forest and farm landscapes where fruiting trees remain available.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not precisely quantified. The species remains broadly distributed within its restricted regional range and is not currently classified as threatened.
